prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current methods for creating animatable head avatars typically rely on a monolithic 3D representation—either explicit meshes or volumetric primitives (such as NeRFs or 3D Gaussian Splatting). This approach is fundamentally flawed because the human head consists of components with contradictory physical characteristics. The face is a distinct, surface-like structure that deforms smoothly, whereas hair consists of thin, high-frequency volumetric geometry. Consequently, single-representation methods force a trade-off: mesh-based approaches fail to render realistic, stranding hair, while volumetric approaches struggle to render the smooth, alias-free surfaces required for high-fidelity skin.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that the optimal solution for high-fidelity head avatars is a **hybrid representation**. We hypothesize that by decoupling the modeling of the face and the hair—assigning a **Neural Mesh** to the face and **3D Gaussian Splatting** to the hair—we can maximize rendering quality for both components simultaneously. Furthermore, we posit that these two distinct rendering pipelines can be seamlessly unified through a novel occlusion-aware blending strategy that resolves depth conflicts between the mesh and the volumetric primitives.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

**1. Facial Modeling (Neural Mesh)**
We will utilize a standard parametric mesh as the geometric foundation for the face to ensure stability.
*   **Geometry Refinement:** To capture details beyond the base parametric model, we will predict a **UV displacement map**. This allows us to apply per-vertex offsets to the mesh, promoting smoothness and detail without increasing computational cost significantly.
*   **Disentangled Neural Textures:** We will employ deferred neural rendering to generate facial colors. We aim to decompose the texture into three logical components: a **diffuse map** (base color), an **expression-dependent map** (dynamic details like wrinkles), and a **view-dependent map** (specular highlights). These will be decoded into RGB values via a lightweight per-pixel decoder.

**2. Hair Modeling (Wearable Gaussians)**
We will adopt 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) for hair to capture high-frequency volumetric structures.
*   **Canonical Representation:** We will construct a static "canonical" hair model from a reference frame.
*   **Animation via Deformation:** To animate the hair, we will apply a two-step transformation: first, a global rigid transformation to track the head's pose, and second, a learned non-rigid deformation field (parameterized by an MLP) to account for hair dynamics and complex movements relative to the scalp.

**3. Occlusion-Aware Blending**
Merging a rasterized mesh and splatted Gaussians creates depth-sorting challenges. We propose a robust blending module:
*   **Robust Depth Testing:** We will implement a "near-z" depth test for the Gaussian hair (using the depth of the first visible Gaussian) rather than integrated depth, ensuring stable occlusion decisions against the solid facial mesh.
*   **Seamless Integration:** We will use early-stopping strategies during Gaussian rendering to discard primitives occluded by the face and apply soft-blending masks at the boundaries (e.g., the hairline) to eliminate visual seams between the rasterized and splatted layers.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Novelty:** This work will be the first to successfully integrate neural meshes and 3D Gaussian Splatting into a unified, differentiable full-head avatar pipeline.
*   **Visual Fidelity:** We expect to eliminate the artifacts common in single-representation models (e.g., skin aliasing in Gaussian models and "helmet-hair" in mesh models).
*   **Versatile Editing:** The strict decoupling of face and hair will naturally facilitate downstream editing tasks, allowing users to swap hairstyles or edit skin textures independently without retraining the entire avatar.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We constructed an experimental framework to evaluate the proposed Hybrid Mesh-Gaussian Head Avatar (MeGA) against state-of-the-art methods. The setup focused on high-fidelity rendering, animation capabilities, and downstream editing tasks.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   We utilized the **NeRSemble dataset**, consisting of multi-view videos of subjects with calibrated camera parameters.
    *   **Data Processing:** Images were downsampled to a resolution of $802 \times 550$. Foreground masks were generated for each image. Facial parsing was performed using an open-source algorithm, and depth maps were generated using Metashape software.
    *   **Splits:** For each subject, we used 9 out of 10 expression sequences and 15 out of 16 available cameras for **training**. The remaining 1 expression sequence and 1 camera were reserved for **evaluation**.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Photorealism/Image Quality:** Evaluated on pixels under the rasterization mask.
        *   **PSNR:** Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (higher is better).
        *   **SSIM:** Structural Similarity Index Measure (higher is better).
        *   **LPIPS:** Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (lower is better).
    *   **Geometry:**
        *   **Geo. MAE:** Mean Absolute Error between the reconstructed depth maps and the rasterized depth maps (lower is better).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **DELTA:** Mesh and NeRF hybrid approach.
    *   **PointAvatar:** Point-based representation.
    *   **Gaussian Head Avatar (GHA):** Dynamic Gaussian method (noted as using a super-resolution module).
    *   **GaussianAvatars:** Rigged 3D Gaussian Splatting representation.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Facial Model:** We employed an enhanced FLAME mesh (densified via four-way subdivision, approximately 16,428 vertices and 40,212 faces) combined with a UV displacement map ($256 \times 256 \times 4$).
    *   **Neural Textures:** We utilized disentangled maps:
        *   Diffuse texture map $\hat { \pmb { T } } _ { d i }$ (learnable parameters).
        *   Dynamic texture map $\hat { \pmb { T } } _ { d y }$ (predicted via CNN conditioned on expression).
        *   View-dependent texture map $\hat { \pmb { T } } _ { v }$ (predicted via CNN conditioned on view vector).
        *   Texture resolution: $1024 \times 1024 \times 4$.
    *   **Pixel Decoder:** A compact MLP with 307 learnable parameters.
    *   **Hair Model:** Canonical hair built using 3D Gaussian Splatting from a single frame, deformed via rigid transformation (ICP) and an MLP-based non-rigid deformation field.
    *   **Occlusion Handling:** We utilized a "near-z" depth threshold (opacity > 0.05) and an early-stopping rendering strategy to manage blending between mesh and Gaussians.
    *   **Editing Optimization:** For texture editing, the diffuse texture map was optimized with a learning rate of 0.01, and the pixel decoder was fine-tuned with a learning rate of 0.0001.

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Table 1: Comparisons with State-of-the-Art Methods on NeRSemble Dataset**
*Aggregated metrics across 9 subjects.*

| Method | Novel-View Synthesis: PSNR $\uparrow$ | Novel-View Synthesis: SSIM $\uparrow$ | Novel-View Synthesis: LPIPS $\downarrow$ | Novel-Expr. Synthesis: PSNR $\uparrow$ | Novel-Expr. Synthesis: SSIM $\uparrow$ | Novel-Expr. Synthesis: LPIPS $\downarrow$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DELTA | 24.62 | 0.871 | 0.138 | 22.60 | 0.858 | 0.158 |
| PointAvatar | 27.08 | 0.918 | 0.091 | 25.79 | 0.916 | 0.103 |
| Gaussian Head Avatar | 29.48 | 0.894 | 0.084 | 22.02 | 0.847 | 0.156 |
| GaussianAvatars | 33.54 | 0.951 | 0.055 | 31.45 | 0.947 | 0.060 |
| **MeGA (Ours)** | **34.11** | **0.954** | **0.052** | **32.59** | **0.949** | **0.057** |

**Table 2: Ablation Studies on Subject 306**
*Impact of specific components on rendering quality and geometric accuracy.*

| Label | Name | Condition / Config | PSNR $\uparrow$ | SSIM $\uparrow$ | LPIPS $\downarrow$ | Geo. MAE $\downarrow$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| (Main) | MeGA (Ours) | Full Model | 33.57 | 0.963 | 0.040 | 2.25 mm |
| (a.1) | MeGA-noview | w/o View Texture ($\hat { \pmb { T } } _ { v }$) | 31.68 | 0.958 | 0.053 | 2.87 mm |
| (a.2) | MeGA-nodyn | w/o Dynamic Texture ($\hat { \pmb { T } } _ { d y }$) | 32.81 | 0.959 | 0.050 | 2.91 mm |
| (b.1) | MeGA-nosubdiv | No mesh subdivision | 32.81 | 0.962 | 0.046 | 3.38 mm |
| (b.2) | MeGA-nodisp | No UV displacement map ($\hat { G } _ { d }$) | 32.99 | 0.959 | 0.054 | 7.48 mm |
| (c.1) | MeGA-gsdepth | Using alpha-accumulated depths | 27.94 | 0.950 | 0.068 | 2.25 mm |
| (c.2) | MeGA-allGS | No early-stopping strategy | 31.42 | 0.957 | 0.048 | 2.25 mm |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Comparisons with Baselines (Visual Analysis)**
*   **Detailed Skin Texture:** We observed that our method captured subtle geometric details, specifically wrinkles (e.g., in Subject 306 and 253), more effectively than baselines due to the expression-dependent dynamic texture map.
*   **Artifacts in Baselines:**
    *   GaussianAvatars (3DGS-based) exhibited blurry or interpenetrated results around the eye and mouth regions (e.g., Subject 304 and 218). We attributed this to the inability of the method to distinguish between eyelid and eyeball Gaussians during the integral-based rendering process.
    *   Gaussian Head Avatar produced promising novel-view synthesis but degraded significantly in novel expression rendering, likely due to reliance on implicit deformation.

**Ablation Analysis Findings**
*   **Texture Components:**
    *   Removing the view-dependent texture map ($\hat { \pmb { T } } _ { v }$) resulted in a failure to capture view-dependent effects, such as highlights in the eyes.
    *   Removing the dynamic texture map ($\hat { \pmb { T } } _ { d y }$) caused a loss of detailed skin appearance, such as forehead wrinkles.
*   **Geometry Components:**
    *   The absence of mesh subdivision restricted the vertex count (approx. 5,023), leading to inferior facial geometry fitting.
    *   The removal of the UV displacement map caused a significant increase in Geometric MAE (from 2.25mm to 7.48mm), reducing the model's ability to capture personalized details.
*   **Blending Strategies:**
    *   Using standard 3DGS-rendered depths for occlusion checks resulted in unstable optimization because the depths fluctuated with minor training errors.
    *   Disabling the "early-stopping" strategy allowed invisible Gaussians (those blocked by the face) to influence the rendering, disrupting facial texture learning and degrading visual quality.

**Editing Capabilities**
*   **Hairstyle Alteration:** We successfully transferred hairstyles between subjects (e.g., Subject A to Subject B) by aligning the Gaussian hair models using ICP with scaling. The rendered avatars maintained high fidelity in novel views.
*   **Texture Editing:** We demonstrated the ability to embed 2D painted modifications (e.g., a logo or tattoo) onto the 3D avatar. By optimizing the diffuse texture map within the masked region, the modifications appeared consistent across novel views and expressions.

[AVAILABLE FIGURES]
### AVAILABLE FIGURES LIST

--------------------------------------------------
Item 3:
  - Filename: figure_1.png
  - Caption: Figure 1. Hybrid Mesh-Gaussian Head Avatar. MeGA models different head components with more suitable representations. For facial modeling, we propose a neural mesh-based representation, including a UV displacement map Ĝd for geometric details, a disentangled neural texture map composed by T̂di, T̂dy , and T̂v to learn the diffuse colors, dynamic textures, and view-dependent colors, respectively. For hair modeling, a canonical 3D Gaussian Splatting is reconstructed and then animated using a rigid transformation and an MLP-based non-rigid deformation field. A mesh occlusion-aware blending is proposed to properly blend the face and hair images. MeGA naturally supports hair alteration and texture editing due to the disentangled representations. Learnable parameters are highlighted using green boxes.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 4:
  - Filename: figure_2.png
  - Caption: Figure 2. Mesh Occlusion-Aware Blending. By comparing the hair “near-z” depth map D̂nz and the head depth map D̂h, we find pixels that should use hair renderings (white regions in Mo). Further combining soft-edge occlusion mask G(Mo) with mesh occlusion-aware hair opacity map Ag which only account for visible Gaussians (i.e., in front of the mesh), we obtain the blending map for final renderings.
--------------------------------------------------

Figures are located in the figures/ directory and should be referenced appropriately in the paper using standard \includegraphics commands.

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

## Example Code for Tables
```latex
\begin{table}
  \centering
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lc@{}}
    \toprule
    Method & Frobnability \\
    \midrule
    Theirs & Frumpy \\
    Yours & Frobbly \\
    Ours & Makes one's heart Frob\\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
  \caption{Results.   Ours is better.}
  \label{tab:example}
\end{table}
```

## Example Code for Figures
```latex
\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{0.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
   %\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{egfigure.eps}

   \caption{Example of caption.
   It is set in Roman so that mathematics (always set in Roman: $B \sin A = A \sin B$) may be included without an ugly clash.}
   \label{fig:onecol}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure*}
  \centering
  \begin{subfigure}{0.68\linewidth}
    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{An example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-a}
  \end{subfigure}
  \hfill
  \begin{subfigure}{0.28\linewidth}
    \fbox{\rule{0pt}{2in} \rule{.9\linewidth}{0pt}}
    \caption{Another example of a subfigure.}
    \label{fig:short-b}
  \end{subfigure}
  \caption{Example of a short caption, which should be centered.}
  \label{fig:short}
\end{figure*}
```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-11.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---
### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.
- Attempt to recall or reconstruct any existing or published paper.
- Use external facts, assumptions, or prior familiarity with the work.
- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.
- Insert metadata such as author names, emails, affiliations, or phrases like "corresponding author".

#### Anonymity Requirement
The paper must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.  
Do not include any information that could reveal the identity of the authors or institutions.

#### Allowed Sources

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Creating high-fidelity, animatable head avatars from multi-view videos is a critical challenge in computer vision. Current methodologies typically rely on a single representation type for the entire head, which creates a fundamental conflict due to the disparate characteristics of head components. The human face consists predominantly of surface-like regions that animate in a low-dimensional space, whereas human hair comprises high-frequency, volumetric thin structures.

Mesh-based representations (e.g., Pixel Codec Avatars) offer excellent control for faces but produce artifacts when rendering hair, often resulting in texture-mapped, surface-like hair appearances. Conversely, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) excels at reconstructing volumetric hair but suffers from aliasing and interpenetration artifacts on the face, particularly during extreme expressions (e.g., jaw opening) or zoom operations. There is currently no single representation capable of simultaneously modeling the surface details of the face and the volumetric complexity of hair without sacrificing the rendering quality of one for the other.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose a **Hybrid Mesh-Gaussian Head Avatar (MeGA)** that decouples the modeling of the human head into its constituent parts using the most appropriate representation for each. We hypothesize that by employing a neural mesh for the face and 3D Gaussian Splatting for the hair, we can achieve photorealistic rendering that surpasses mono-representation approaches.

Our core technical strategy involves:
1.  **Facial Modeling:** Using an enhanced FLAME mesh with a predicted UV displacement map and disentangled neural textures to capture surface geometry and dynamic appearance.
2.  **Hair Modeling:** Using a canonical 3DGS representation deformed by a rigid transformation and a non-rigid MLP deformation field.
3.  **Hybrid Blending:** Implementing an occlusion-aware blending mechanism based on "near-z" depth to resolve depth ordering conflicts between the explicit mesh and volumetric Gaussians.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will construct an animatable avatar driven by FLAME parameters (shape $\beta$, expression $\psi$, and pose $\phi$) and a view vector $\mathbf{d}$. The system will consist of three distinct modules: Animatable Facial Mesh, Wearable Gaussian Hair, and Occlusion-Aware Blending.

### 1. Animatable Facial Mesh
To model the face, we will employ an enhanced FLAME mesh $\mathcal{T}$ containing subdivision-densified faces and added geometry for teeth. The vertices $\mathcal{V}$ will be calculated via Linear Blend Skinning (LBS):
$$ \mathcal{T}(\beta, \psi, \phi) = \{ \mathcal{V}(\beta, \psi, \phi), \mathcal{F} \} $$
where $\mathcal{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{16428 \times 3}$ represents the vertices derived from shape $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{300}$, expression $\psi \in \mathbb{R}^{100}$, and pose $\phi \in \mathbb{R}^{15}$.

**Geometry Refinement:**
To capture geometric details beyond the standard FLAME space, we will predict a UV displacement map $\hat{G}_d$ conditioned on $\psi$ and $\phi$. We define the refined mesh $\mathcal{T}_r$ as:
$$ \mathcal{T}_r(\beta, \psi, \phi) = \{ \mathcal{V}_r(\beta, \psi, \phi), \mathcal{F} \} $$
$$ \mathcal{V}_r(\beta, \psi, \phi) = \mathcal{V}(\beta, \psi, \phi) + \mathcal{S}(\hat{G}_d) $$
Here, $\mathcal{S}(\cdot)$ samples values based on UV coordinates. This approach leverages the locality of CNNs to promote smoothness and supports unlimited mesh resolution.

**Disentangled Neural Texture & Decoding:**
We will implement deferred neural rendering using a texture map $\hat{\pmb{T}} \in \mathbb{R}^{1024 \times 1024 \times 4}$ disentangled into three components:
1.  **Diffuse Texture ($\hat{\pmb{T}}_{di}$):** Static learnable parameters for base color.
2.  **View Texture ($\hat{\pmb{T}}_{v}$):** Predicted via CNN conditioned on view vector $\mathbf{d}$.
3.  **Dynamic Texture ($\hat{\pmb{T}}_{dy}$):** Predicted via CNN conditioned on expression $\psi$.

A compact pixel decoder MLP (approx. 307 parameters) will decode these textures into RGB colors based solely on UV coordinates, excluding XYZ inputs to prevent overfitting to specific coordinate systems.

### 2. Wearable Gaussian Hair
We will model hair using 3D Gaussian Splatting to capture volumetric structures.
**Canonical Representation:**
We will optimize a canonical 3DGS set $\mathcal{G}_c = \{ x_c^i, r_c^i, s_c^i, o_c^i, sh_c^i \}_{i=1:N}$ from a single reference frame. The rendering color $C$ for a pixel is defined by alpha blending sorted Gaussians:
$$ C = \sum_{i} c_i \alpha'_i \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'_j) $$
where $c_i$ is the color from spherical harmonics and $\alpha'_i$ is the blending weight derived from opacity $o^i$ and 2D projection.

**Rigid and Non-Rigid Deformation:**
To animate the hair, we will first compute a rigid transformation $(R_i, t_i)$ for each frame relative to the canonical frame using Iterative Closest Point (ICP) on scalp vertices:
$$ (R_i, t_i) = \mathrm{ICP}(\mathcal{V}^{scalp}(\beta_i, \psi_i, \phi_i), \mathcal{V}^{scalp}(\beta_c, \psi_c, \phi_c)) $$
Subsequently, to capture non-rigid dynamics, we will learn a deformation field parameterized by an MLP $\mathcal{M}_d$ conditioned on expression parameters:
$$ \mathcal{M}_d : \psi \rightarrow (\delta x, \delta r, \delta s, \delta o, \delta sh) $$
The final animated Gaussian parameters will be the sum of the rigid-transformed canonical parameters and these learned deltas.

### 3. Occlusion-Aware Blending
To resolve the depth conflict between the mesh face and Gaussian hair, we will implement a "near-z" depth test rather than using integrated GS depth. We define "near-z" depth $\hat{D}_{nz}$ as the depth of the first Gaussian (depth-sorted) with opacity $> 0.05$.

We will generate a binary occlusion mask $M_o = \hat{D}_{nz} < \hat{D}_{h}$, where $\hat{D}_{h}$ is the rasterized mesh depth. To prevent artifacts:
1.  **Early-Stopping:** During Gaussian rendering, we will terminate alpha accumulation if the next Gaussian is physically too far (on the other side of the head).
2.  **Soft-Blending:** We will apply Gaussian smoothing to $M_o$ to create a soft-edge mask $G(M_o)$.

The final image $\hat{I}$ will be synthesized as:
$$ \hat{I} = \hat{A}_{hair} \cdot \hat{I}_{hair} + (\mathbf{1} - \hat{A}_{hair}) \cdot \hat{I}_{head} $$
where $\hat{A}_{hair} := \mathcal{A}_g \cdot G(M_o)$ represents the blended alpha map.

### 4. Optimization Framework
Optimization will proceed in three stages:
1.  **Facial Mesh Optimization:** Optimizing texture maps and displacement with photometric losses, geometric losses (depth/normal), and a specific **Shrink Loss** to pull scalp vertices inward to avoid hair intersection:
    $$ \mathcal{L}_{shr}^F = || \mathcal{V}_r^{scalp} - \mathrm{Mean}(\mathcal{V}^{scalp}) ||_2 $$
2.  **Canonical Hair Optimization:** Optimizing 3DGS parameters with appearance losses and a **Silhouette Loss** to ensure disentanglement:
    $$ \mathcal{L}_{silh}^H = || (M_{hair} - \hat{A}_{hair}) \odot \Delta ||_1 $$
3.  **Joint Optimization:** Fine-tuning all parameters, including the deformation MLP, with an as-isometric-as-possible (AIAP) regularization to maintain hair rigidity.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Hybrid Architecture:** We define the first hybrid representation for full-head avatars that utilizes Neural Mesh for facial precision and 3DGS for hair volume, theoretically eliminating the trade-offs present in single-representation systems.
2.  **Disentangled Texture Formulation:** By separating diffuse, view-dependent, and dynamic textures, we expect to achieve higher fidelity in skin rendering (e.g., dynamic wrinkles) compared to standard neural textures.
3.  **Robust Blending Mechanism:** The proposed occlusion-aware blending with "near-z" depth will provide a theoretical solution to the open problem of compositing explicit surfaces with volumetric primitives without depth artifacts.
4.  **Downstream Versatility:** The explicit decomposition of the head structure will inherently support semantic editing tasks, such as hairstyle transfer and texture painting, which are difficult in fully implicit representations.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
